questions.question: What is the primary difference between the 'async' and 'defer' attributes when loading external scripts?
questions.code:
<!-- Option A / B example -->
<script src="app.js" async></script>
<script src="analytics.js" defer></script>
options: 'async' executes as soon as downloaded; 'defer' waits until HTML parsing is complete.
'defer' executes as soon as downloaded; 'async' waits for DOMContentLoaded.
'async' blocks HTML parsing completely while 'defer' downloads in the background.
Both attributes behave identically in modern browsers.
questions.explanation: 'async' scripts download asynchronously and execute the moment download finishes, pausing HTML parsing. 'defer' scripts download in parallel but execute strictly after HTML parsing completes, in document order.
questions.simpleExplanation: Imagine downloading a movie: 'async' pauses dinner immediately to watch it the moment it finishes downloading; 'defer' downloads quietly and waits until dinner is completely over before starting.

questions.question: Which HTML5 semantic element is best suited for content that is self-contained and could be syndicated independently?
options: <section>
<article>
<aside>
<div>
questions.explanation: The <article> tag specifies independent, self-contained content that makes sense on its own (like a blog post, news story, or forum comment). <section> is for generic thematic grouping.
questions.simpleExplanation: An <article> is like a newspaper clipping—you can cut it out and read it anywhere and it still makes complete sense by itself.

questions.question: How does 'localStorage' differ from 'sessionStorage' in the browser?
options: localStorage data expires when the tab is closed; sessionStorage persists indefinitely.
sessionStorage data expires when the browser tab closes; localStorage has no expiration time.
localStorage is limited to 4KB while sessionStorage supports up to 5MB.
sessionStorage is sent to the server with every HTTP request, whereas localStorage is not.
questions.explanation: localStorage persists across browser sessions until explicitly deleted by the user or code. sessionStorage only lasts for the duration of the page session (cleared when the tab/window is closed).
questions.simpleExplanation: sessionStorage is like writing on a restaurant napkin that gets thrown away when you leave; localStorage is like writing in a permanent notebook you keep in your backpack.

questions.question: Which of the following is considered a 'void' (self-closing) element in HTML5?
options: <span>
<input>
<button>
questions.explanation:
Void elements in HTML cannot have any child nodes or content between opening and closing tags. Examples include , ,
,
, and .
questions.simpleExplanation: Void elements are like one-piece stickers—you just stick them on the page; you can't put anything inside them.

questions.question: Why is the 'alt' attribute essential on an element?
options: It defines the tooltip shown when hovering over the image.
It provides fallback text for screen readers and when the image fails to load.
It caches the image URL in the browser memory for faster reloads.
It sets the default aspect ratio before the image dimensions are downloaded.
questions.explanation: The 'alt' attribute provides alternative text used by accessibility tools (like screen readers for visually impaired users) and displays if the image file fails to load or load is blocked.
questions.simpleExplanation: The 'alt' tag is like an audio description for someone who cannot see the picture, or a placeholder label if the picture frame arrives empty.

questions.question: With 'box-sizing: border-box', what will be the total rendered width of the element?
options: 200px
250px
225px
240px
questions.explanation: With 'box-sizing: border-box', the specified width includes content, padding, and border. Thus, total rendered width remains exactly 200px; the content area shrinks to accommodate the 20px padding and 5px border.
questions.simpleExplanation: border-box is like ordering a suitcase that must fit in a 200px overhead locker—the padding and border fit inside the suitcase, rather than making the suitcase bulge outside.

questions.question: Which CSS selector has the highest specificity?
questions.code:
/* Which one wins? */
#navbar .item a
header nav.menu a
nav ul li.item
.navbar .menu .item a
options: #navbar .item a
header nav.menu a
nav ul li.item
.navbar .menu .item a
questions.explanation: Specificity is calculated as (Inline, IDs, Classes/Attributes/Pseudo-classes, Elements). '#navbar .item a' has 1 ID, 1 class, 1 element (1, 1, 1), beating selectors that only use classes and elements.
questions.simpleExplanation: An ID (#) is like an Aadhaar or passport number—it outranks any number of job titles or descriptions (classes).

questions.question: What is the difference between 'justify-content' and 'align-items' in CSS Flexbox?
options: 'justify-content' aligns items along the cross axis; 'align-items' aligns along the main axis.
'justify-content' aligns along the main axis; 'align-items' aligns along the cross axis.
Both properties align along the main axis, but 'align-items' applies only to multi-line flex containers.
'justify-content' is only for text, while 'align-items' is only for div blocks.
questions.explanation: In Flexbox, 'justify-content' controls alignment along the main axis (horizontal by default for row), while 'align-items' controls alignment along the perpendicular cross axis (vertical for row).
questions.simpleExplanation: In a horizontal row, justify-content decides where items sit left-to-right, while align-items decides whether they sit high, low, or centered top-to-bottom.

questions.question: An element with 'position: absolute' is positioned relative to which ancestor?
options: Always relative to the <body> element.
Its nearest ancestor with a 'position' other than 'static'.
Its direct parent regardless of the parent's position value.
The viewport window.
questions.explanation: An absolutely positioned element looks up the DOM tree and positions itself relative to the nearest ancestor that has a position property set to relative, absolute, fixed, or sticky. If none exists, it defaults to the initial containing block (viewport/html).
questions.simpleExplanation: The child element looks up its family tree until it finds the first parent with a set boundary (relative/absolute); if nobody claims it, it anchors to the entire screen.

questions.question: What does the following CSS Grid rule achieve?
options: It creates exactly 3 columns that stay 200px wide.
It creates a responsive grid where columns automatically wrap and stretch to fill remaining space.
It limits the grid to a maximum of 200 columns.
It forces every item to be fixed at 200px without expanding.
questions.explanation: 'auto-fit' combined with 'minmax(200px, 1fr)' automatically creates as many 200px columns as can fit in the row. As the screen expands or shrinks, columns wrap and expand (1fr) without needing media queries.
questions.simpleExplanation: It's like an elastic shelf: as long as each book has at least 200px of space, it packs as many books per shelf as possible and stretches them neatly to fill gaps.

questions.question: What will be printed to the console?
questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (1, 4). Next, microtasks (Promise.then) run before macrotasks (setTimeout). Therefore, 3 logs before 2, giving '1, 4, 3, 2'.
questions.simpleExplanation: Synchronous tasks are customers already at the counter (1 and 4). Promises are VIP tickets (microtasks, 3) who skip regular line. setTimeout goes to the back of the normal queue (macrotask, 2).

questions.question: What is the output of this code snippet?
options: undefined, undefined, undefined
questions.explanation: 'var' is function-scoped, not block-scoped. By the time the setTimeout callbacks execute after 100ms, the loop has completed and the shared 'i' variable holds the final value 3.
questions.simpleExplanation: Because 'var' shares one single sticky note, by the time the timer rings 100ms later, the note has already been overwritten with the number 3.

questions.question: What happens when you access a 'let' or 'const' variable before its declaration?
options: Both log 'undefined'.
myVar logs 'undefined', and myLet throws a ReferenceError.
Both throw a ReferenceError.
myVar throws a ReferenceError, and myLet logs 'undefined'.
questions.explanation: 'var' is hoisted and initialized with 'undefined'. 'let' and 'const' are also hoisted, but they remain uninitialized in the 'Temporal Dead Zone' (TDZ) until the declaration is evaluated, throwing a ReferenceError.
questions.simpleExplanation: 'var' is like reserving an empty chair before someone arrives. 'let' puts caution tape around the chair until the person actually sits down—touching it triggers an alarm.

questions.question: How do arrow functions handle the 'this' keyword compared to regular functions?
options: Arrow functions have their own dynamically bound 'this'.
Arrow functions lexically inherit 'this' from their enclosing outer scope.
Arrow functions always bind 'this' to the current object literal.
There is no difference between them regarding 'this'.
questions.explanation: Arrow functions do not bind their own 'this'. Instead, they inherit 'this' lexically from the scope in which they were defined. In an object literal, the enclosing scope is usually global (or undefined in strict mode).
questions.simpleExplanation: Regular functions take their identity ('this') from whoever called them. Arrow functions are loyal to where they were born and keep their parent scope's 'this'.

questions.question: What is the result of the following comparison?
questions.code:
console.log([] == false);
console.log([] === false);
options: true, true
true, false
false, false
false, true
questions.explanation: With '==', type coercion converts [] to an empty string '', and false to 0. '' == 0 coerces to 0 == 0, which is true. Strict equality '===' checks both type (object vs boolean) and returns false.
questions.simpleExplanation: '==' does crazy conversions behind your back to make them look comparable. '===' checks both value and type without converting, noticing immediately that a list is not a boolean.

questions.question: What library provides the event loop, thread pool, and cross-platform asynchronous I/O in Node.js?
options: V8
libuv
npm
OpenSSL
questions.explanation: While V8 executes JavaScript code, libuv is the multi-platform C library that handles Node's event loop, asynchronous DNS resolution, file system operations, and worker thread pool.
questions.simpleExplanation: V8 is the brain that understands JavaScript instructions, while libuv is the tireless engine crew in the background that handles file reading and network requests.

questions.question: Why are Streams preferred over 'fs.readFile' when handling large files in Node.js?
options: Streams encrypt file contents automatically during transfer.
Streams process data in chunks without loading the entire file into memory.
fs.readFile is asynchronous, while Streams are always synchronous.
Streams bypass the Node.js event loop completely.
questions.explanation: 'fs.readFile' loads the entire file into RAM as a single Buffer before invoking the callback, which can crash the process with Out of Memory errors. Streams read and transmit data chunk-by-chunk with minimal memory footprint.
questions.simpleExplanation: Reading with fs.readFile is like trying to drink a whole gallon jug in one gulp. Streaming is like sipping it through a straw as it flows.

questions.question: In what order will the callbacks execute in this Node.js script?
options: 'Immediate' always executes before 'Tick'.
'Tick' runs first because process.nextTick fires right after the current operation before the event loop continues.
'Timeout' always runs before 'Tick'.
The execution order is completely random.
questions.explanation: 'process.nextTick' is not technically part of the event loop; it runs immediately after the current JavaScript execution completes, ahead of all event loop phases (timers, I/O, check/immediate).
questions.simpleExplanation: process.nextTick is like whispering 'do this next before you take another step' to the chef, so it happens right away.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between CommonJS and ES Modules in Node.js?
options: CommonJS loads modules synchronously at runtime; ES Modules are statically analyzed and can be loaded asynchronously.
CommonJS is supported only in browsers, while ESM is only for Node.js.
ES Modules do not support top-level await.
CommonJS requires a transpiler like Babel, while ESM does not.
questions.explanation: CommonJS 'require()' executes synchronously when reached in the code. ES Modules ('import') are static, enabling static analysis, tree-shaking, and asynchronous module graph evaluation.
questions.simpleExplanation: require() is like ordering groceries at the cash counter when you realize you need them. ESM is like handing your grocery list before entering the store so they can prepare everything efficiently.

questions.question: When should you use the 'worker_threads' module instead of the 'cluster' module in Node.js?
options: When handling high I/O traffic with multiple network sockets.
When performing heavy CPU-bound computations that benefit from shared memory.
When you want each worker to run as a separate OS process with its own memory.
worker_threads are deprecated and should not be used.
questions.explanation: The 'cluster' module forks separate Node.js processes (ideal for scaling HTTP servers across CPU cores). The 'worker_threads' module runs multiple threads inside a single process, enabling shared memory for CPU-heavy tasks like cryptography or image processing.
questions.simpleExplanation: Cluster is like hiring separate workers at separate desks. Worker threads are like two people sitting at the same desk sharing the same notebook.

questions.question: What happens if a middleware function does not call 'next()' or send a response?
options: Express automatically passes the request to the next handler after 5 seconds.
The request hangs indefinitely until the client times out.
An uncaught Exception is thrown immediately.
Express returns a default 200 OK status.
questions.explanation: In Express, every middleware must either terminate the request-response cycle (e.g. res.send/res.json) or call next() to pass control. Otherwise, the request will hang until the client socket times out.
questions.simpleExplanation: Middleware is like an assembly line station. If a worker inspects the package but neither passes it to the next person nor ships it out, the conveyor belt just stops.

questions.question: How do you define an error-handling middleware in Express?
options: app.use((req, res, err) => { ... })
app.use((err, req, res, next) => { ... })
app.catch((error) => { ... })
app.onError((req, res) => { ... })
questions.explanation: Express identifies error-handling middleware strictly by its function arity: it must take exactly 4 parameters: '(err, req, res, next)'. Even if you don't use 'next', it must be declared.
questions.simpleExplanation: Express looks specifically for four seats at the table (err, req, res, next). If you only provide three, Express thinks it's a regular route handler rather than an emergency team.

questions.question: Given the route '/users/:id?role=admin', how do you access 'id' and 'role'?
options: req.body.id and req.body.role
req.params.id and req.query.role
req.query.id and req.params.role
req.headers.id and req.headers.role
questions.explanation: Route parameters defined in the path with a colon (':id') are accessed via 'req.params.id'. Query string parameters following the question mark ('?role=admin') are accessed via 'req.query.role'.
questions.simpleExplanation: Route parameters (:id) are part of the house address. Query parameters (?role=admin) are extra instructions written on the delivery package.

questions.question: What is the purpose of 'express.json()' built-in middleware?
questions.code: app.use(express.json());
options: It validates that outgoing responses are valid JSON.
It parses incoming requests with JSON payloads and populates 'req.body'.
It stringifies JavaScript objects before sending them to the database.
It compresses JSON responses using gzip.
questions.explanation: 'express.json()' is a built-in middleware based on body-parser. It inspects incoming HTTP requests with Content-Type 'application/json' and parses the raw body buffer into a JavaScript object under 'req.body'.
questions.simpleExplanation: It's like an automated translator that unpacks JSON packages coming from the frontend and turns them into ready-to-use JavaScript objects.

questions.question: Why do browser-based frontend apps require CORS headers from an Express backend?
questions.code:
const cors = require('cors');
app.use(cors());
options: To encrypt passwords transferred via HTTP.
To satisfy the browser's Same-Origin Policy when making cross-origin requests.
To speed up database connection pools.
To allow server-sent events (SSE) over WebSockets.
questions.explanation: Browsers enforce the Same-Origin Policy for security. If the frontend is hosted on 'localhost:3000' and requests 'localhost:5000', the browser blocks the response unless the server explicitly sends Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) headers.
questions.simpleExplanation: CORS headers are like the backend giving a security guest pass to the browser, saying: 'Yes, I allow requests coming from this other website domain.'

questions.question: What is the main difference between 'git merge' and 'git rebase'?
questions.code:
git merge feature
# vs
git rebase main
options: 'merge' preserves the exact historical timeline with a merge commit; 'rebase' rewrites commit history linearly.
'rebase' creates a new commit combining branches; 'merge' deletes the source branch.
'merge' can only be done locally; 'rebase' can only be done on GitHub.
There is no difference; they are aliases for the same operation.
questions.explanation: 'git merge' joins two branches together and records a merge commit, preserving true commit timestamps. 'git rebase' replays commits from the current branch onto the tip of another branch, producing a clean, linear commit history.
questions.simpleExplanation: Merge is like two roads joining together with an intersection. Rebase is like picking up your section of the road and paving it right onto the end of the highway.

questions.question: How do 'git reset --hard' and 'git revert' differ when undoing a commit?
questions.code:
git reset --hard HEAD~1
# vs
git revert HEAD
options: 'revert' permanently deletes commit history, while 'reset' creates a new commit.
'reset --hard' alters commit history and deletes uncommitted changes; 'revert' creates a new commit that safely inverts the changes.
'revert' only works on staged files; 'reset' only works on pushed branches.
Both commands do exactly the same thing.
questions.explanation: 'git reset --hard' rewinds HEAD to an earlier commit and discards changes in working directory (dangerous for shared branches). 'git revert' creates a new public commit with inverse changes, leaving history intact.
questions.simpleExplanation: Reset is like ripping the last page out of the history book. Revert is like writing a new page that says: 'Cancel the instructions from the previous page.'

questions.question: What command allows you to temporarily save uncommitted changes without committing them?
options: git branch save
git stash
git archive
git checkout --temp
questions.explanation: 'git stash' records the current state of the working directory and index (staged changes), rolling back to a clean working directory so you can switch branches. 'git stash pop' restores them later.
questions.simpleExplanation: git stash is like putting all your current work-in-progress papers into a drawer so your desk is clean, and pulling them back out when you're ready.

questions.question: What does 'git fetch' do compared to 'git pull'?
questions.code:
git fetch origin
# vs
git pull origin main
options: 'fetch' downloads remote commits without merging them into your current branch; 'pull' fetches and automatically merges.
'fetch' deletes local branches not on remote; 'pull' creates them.
'fetch' uploads your commits; 'pull' downloads them.
'fetch' is only for Git tags, while 'pull' is for branches.
questions.explanation: 'git fetch' queries the remote repository and downloads new commits and refs without modifying your local working tree. 'git pull' is effectively 'git fetch' followed immediately by 'git merge'.
questions.simpleExplanation: Fetch is like downloading your mail into your mailbox to look at when you want. Pull downloads the mail and opens it right on your desk immediately.

questions.question: If a file was already committed to Git, what must you do after adding it to '.gitignore' so Git stops tracking it?
questions.code:
git rm --cached <file>
git commit -m "Stop tracking <file>"
options: Simply adding it to .gitignore is sufficient; Git stops tracking immediately.
Delete the file physically from the operating system disk.
Run 'git rm --cached <file>' to remove it from the index, then commit.
Rename the repository on GitHub.
questions.explanation: '.gitignore' only prevents untracked files from being added. If a file is already tracked, Git continues tracking it until you remove it from the staging index with 'git rm --cached'.
questions.simpleExplanation: .gitignore only stops new things from entering the guest list. If someone is already inside the party, you have to formally walk them out (git rm --cached).

questions.question: What is the primary difference between horizontal and vertical database scaling?
options: Vertical scaling adds more machines (sharding); horizontal scaling upgrades CPU/RAM on a single machine.
Horizontal scaling adds more servers/nodes to share the load; vertical scaling adds more CPU/RAM/storage to an existing server.
Vertical scaling is only possible with NoSQL; horizontal scaling is only for SQL.
Horizontal scaling is always cheaper than vertical scaling.
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling (scaling up) means upgrading the hardware of a single machine. Horizontal scaling (scaling out) means adding multiple commodity servers (via clustering or sharding) to distribute workloads.
questions.simpleExplanation: Vertical scaling is making a courier driver run faster by buying him a sports car. Horizontal scaling is hiring five more delivery drivers.

questions.question: In the context of REST APIs, what does it mean for an HTTP method to be 'Idempotent'?
questions.code:
GET /items/1
PUT /items/1
DELETE /items/1
options: The method returns data in encrypted format.
Calling the method multiple times produces the same server state as calling it once.
The method can only be executed by authenticated users.
The response is guaranteed to be cached by the browser.
questions.explanation: An idempotent HTTP method (like GET, PUT, DELETE) can be executed multiple times without changing the result beyond the initial application. POST is typically NOT idempotent because repeating it creates multiple resources.
questions.simpleExplanation: Pressing an elevator button for floor 3 five times still sends the elevator to floor 3 (idempotent). But clicking 'Buy Now' five times could charge your card five times (non-idempotent).

questions.question: What are the three parts of a JSON Web Token (JWT)?
questions.code: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIiwibmFtZSI6IkpvaG4ifQ.SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJV_adQssw5c
options: Username, Password, and Role
Header, Payload, and Signature
Client ID, Client Secret, and Token
Public Key, Private Key, and Salt
questions.explanation: A JWT consists of three Base64URL-encoded strings separated by dots: Header (algorithm & token type), Payload (user claims and expiration timestamp), and Signature (verifies integrity with secret/private key).
questions.simpleExplanation: A JWT is like a sealed festival wristband: the Header describes the band type, the Payload has your VIP tier info, and the tamper-proof security stamp (Signature) proves it wasn't forged.

questions.question: How does the 'Cache-Aside' (Lazy Loading) caching pattern work?
options: The database writes data directly to the cache every night.
The application first checks the cache; on a miss, it reads from the DB and stores the result in the cache.
All writes go to the cache first, and an asynchronous worker updates the DB later.
The cache intercepts all queries and manages database transactions.
questions.explanation: In Cache-Aside, the app first checks Redis/Memcached. If data is found (cache hit), it returns it. If not (cache miss), it queries the database, writes the fetched data into the cache for future requests, and returns it.
questions.simpleExplanation: Before walking to the library (database), you check your desk drawer (cache). If the book isn't in your drawer, you get it from the library and leave a copy in your drawer for next time.

questions.question: What is the primary trade-off of adding database indexes (e.g., B-Tree index) to a table?
questions.code: CREATE INDEX idx_user_email ON users(email);
options: Indexes speed up SELECT queries, but slow down INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations and consume extra storage.
Indexes speed up INSERT queries, but cause SELECT queries to lock the table.
Indexes eliminate the need for foreign keys.
Indexes automatically encrypt sensitive database columns.
questions.explanation: Indexes drastically accelerate read queries by avoiding full table scans. However, every write operation (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) must update both the table data and all associated index trees, adding latency and disk usage.
questions.simpleExplanation: The index at the back of a textbook lets you find topics instantly, but every time the author adds a new paragraph, they have to rewrite and reorder that entire index.

questions.question: What does RAG stand for in the context of Large Language Models?
options: Relational Augmented Graph
Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Recursive Attention Gradient
Reinforced Automated Generation
questions.explanation: RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. It enhances LLM responses by fetching relevant factual documents from an external knowledge base and passing them as context inside the prompt.
questions.simpleExplanation: Traditional LLMs take a closed-book test using only memory. RAG turns it into an open-book test by looking up the exact textbook page before answering.

questions.question: Why is 'chunking with overlap' used when preparing text documents for a RAG vector database?
options: To encrypt document chunks to comply with GDPR.
To prevent loss of contextual meaning and semantic continuity at chunk boundaries.
To compress the file size before uploading to AWS S3.
To reduce the number of vector dimensions in the embedding model.
questions.explanation: If a text is cut cleanly without overlap, a sentence or idea that spans across the cut will lose its context. Adding an overlap (e.g. 10-20% tokens) ensures surrounding context is preserved in both adjacent chunks.
questions.simpleExplanation: When taking panoramic photos, you slightly overlap the edges of each photo so the final stitched picture doesn't have missing seams or cut-off landmarks.

questions.question: How are text queries compared against document chunks inside a Vector Database?
options: By performing exact SQL LIKE string matching.
By converting both query and chunks into mathematical vector embeddings and calculating distance (e.g., Cosine Similarity).
By hashing words with MD5 and checking collision tables.
By counting character occurrences using regex.
questions.explanation: Text chunks and queries are passed through an embedding model that maps semantic meaning into high-dimensional vectors. Vector databases use algorithms like Cosine Similarity or Euclidean distance to retrieve chunks with the closest mathematical meaning.
questions.simpleExplanation: Instead of looking for exact matching words, embeddings place 'puppy' and 'dog' close to each other on a multi-dimensional concept map.

questions.question: What is an LLM 'hallucination' and how does RAG help mitigate it?
options: Hallucination is when an LLM runs out of GPU memory; RAG increases the hardware memory limit.
Hallucination is when an LLM generates plausibly sounding but false information; RAG grounds generation in retrieved verified source text.
Hallucination is when an API token expires; RAG automatically refreshes JWTs.
Hallucination occurs when an LLM translates between different languages.
questions.explanation: Hallucinations occur because LLMs predict next tokens statistically rather than checking factual databases. RAG provides verified source documents in the prompt context, forcing the model to cite and synthesize real retrieved data.
questions.simpleExplanation: Hallucination is when someone confidently invents a convincing story because they don't know the answer. RAG hands them the verified fact sheet so they don't have to guess.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'Re-ranker' (Cross-Encoder) stage in an advanced RAG pipeline?
questions.code: Query -> Dense Retrieval (Top 50) -> Re-Ranker (Top 5) -> LLM
options: To re-write the user's prompt in different languages.
To re-score and precisely re-order the top retrieved documents based on deep query-document cross-attention.
To permanently delete low-ranking chunks from the vector database.
To fine-tune the LLM weights in real time.
questions.explanation: Bi-encoder vector search is fast across millions of chunks but approximate. A Re-ranker (Cross-Encoder) takes the top 30-50 candidates and scores full token-level query-document interactions to ensure only the highest relevance chunks reach the LLM's limited context window.
questions.simpleExplanation: A fast metal detector scans the whole beach and finds 50 metal objects; a jeweler then carefully inspects those 50 items up close to pick out only the 3 real gold rings.
